WASF-RAG: A Workflow-Aware SchedulingFramework with Retrieval-Augmented Generationfor Performance-Heterogeneous, Multi-GenerationalHPCAbstract—In multi-generational High-PerformanceComputing(HPC) systems, scientific workflow scheduling facesthe dual challenges of complex task dependencies and highlyheterogeneous resource performance. Existing heuristicalgorithms (such as HEFT and Min-Min) rely on staticassumptions, making them difficult to adapt to dynamicenvironments; meanwhile, although Deep ReinforcementLearning (DRL) holds potential for decision modeling, it haslong been constrained by issues such as slow trainingconvergence, sparse rewards, and non-stationarity in staterepresentation. To address these challenges, this paper proposesWASF-RAG, a retrieval-augmented scheduling frameworktailored for HPC. The framework reformulates scheduling as adecision sequence generation problem, utilizing a mixed-strategy knowledge base constructed offline to provide stablevalue priors for online learning. By decoupling therepresentation spaces of retrieval and policy, WASF-RAGensures metric consistency in experience reuse. Furthermore, itincorporates a Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)mechanism to transform retrieved historical expert trajectoriesinto dense feedback signals, thereby effectively overcoming thecold-start dilemma. High-fidelity simulation experimentsdemonstrate that in extreme scenarios with constrained I/Obandwidth, the framework autonomously learns Data Localitystrategies, reducing the makespan by up to 63.5% compared tothe HEFT algorithm. Ablation studies indicate that theproposed retrieval-augmented mechanism significantlyoutperforms pure DRL scheduling approaches, demonstratingclear performance advantages in extremely heterogeneousscenarios and effectively enhancing algorithmic robustness.Across extensive test sets, WASF-RAG achieves an averageperformance improvement of 21.7%, validating its effectivenessin complex dynamic environments.Keywords—Workflow Scheduling, Deep ReinforcementLearning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Graph NeuralNetworks, Potential-Based Reward ShapingI. INTRODUCTIONWith the rapid iteration of High-Performance Computing(HPC) hardware, modern data centers universally exhibit a"multi-generational" characteristic where new and legacynodes coexist, constituting a resource environment that ishighly heterogeneous and uneven in performance. Suchenvironments must support scientific workflows withcomplex dependencies—such as astrophysical simulations [1]and seismic imaging [2]—making scheduling onperformance-asymmetric resources with the objective ofminimizing makespan a typical NP-hard problem [3].The evolution of solutions to this problem has progressedfrom theoretical models to engineering heuristics. Earlyresearch mostly constructed theoretical models based onqueuing theory or linear programming. However, in realproduction environments facing issues such as I/O contention,network congestion, or multi-tenant interference, their staticassumptions regarding task execution times andcommunication overheads often fail to hold. Consequently,the industry has long relied on list-based heuristic algorithmssuch as HEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. Although these methodsare widely deployed due to their low computational overheadand ease of implementation, they are essentially rigidsimplifications of complex dynamic systems. Once real-worldscenarios deviate from preset models (e.g., encounteringsevere resource fragmentation or performance jitter), theperformance of such static methods declines sharply, leadingto significant efficiency losses [6].To break the constraints of static assumptions, theacademic community has begun exploring the use of DeepReinforcement Learning (DRL) and Graph Neural Networks(GNN) [7] to build data-driven schedulers. Methods such asGrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9] have demonstrated thepotential to surpass static rules in certain scenarios byperceiving topological structures and learning end-to-endpolicies [10]. However, such learning-based methods still facethe dilemma of sample-inefficient exploration in practicaldeployment. On one hand, the state representation of GNNsdrifts continuously as the policy updates (Non-stationarity)[11], making it difficult to effectively reuse historicalexperience. On the other hand, the inherent reward sparsity ofscheduling tasks [12], [13] leads to extremely slow modelconvergence. This often results in poor agent performanceduring the cold-start phase, making it difficult to meet thestrict stability and real-time requirements of productionenvironments.The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigmoffers a new opportunity to address the instability of theaforementioned sequential decision-making [14]. Themassive volume of high-quality scheduling logs accumulatedover long-term operations in HPC data centers actuallyconstitutes a rich, underexploited repository of decision-making data. Unlike high-latency generative schedulingmethods [15], we advocate using these logs as "externalmemory" to reuse historical expert experience via retrieval,while guaranteeing real-time inference. Based on this, thispaper proposes WASF-RAG—a retrieval-augmentedscheduling framework tailored for HPC.To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we designeda decoupled dual-GNN architecture: it utilizes a frozenretrieval encoder to construct a time-invariant metric space,ensuring the stable retrieval of high-value reference statesfrom the historical library. Simultaneously, it combines aPotential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) mechanism totransform retrieved expert trajectories into immediate dense

Ourextensive experimental evaluation, conducted within SimGrid[16] / WRENCH [17] shows that WASF-RAG not onlypossesses performance comparable to the best heuristics understeady-state conditions but also exhibits significantadvantages in extreme heterogeneous scenarios withconstrained I/O bandwidth. RELATED WORKA. From Static Rules to Dynamic Scheduling MechanismsIn multi-generational HPC systems, early researchprimarily relied on list-based heuristic algorithms such asHEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. These methods are widelyadopted in practice due to their controllable computationaloverhead and ease of implementation. However, assummarized in Table 1, such static methods heavily rely onestimates of task execution times and communicationoverheads, which are typically based on idealized assumptionsof the system state.B. Scheduling Methods based on Deep ReinforcementLearning and Graph Neural NetworksDeep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a pathway forend-to-end optimization in online scheduling. DeepRM [13]validated the feasibility of learning-based policies in resourceallocation scenarios, but its capability was constrained by alack of structural representation for task dependencies.Subsequently, works such as GrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9]utilized Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode thetopological structure of workflow Directed Acyclic Graph(DAG), enabling agents to make decisions guided bystructural information. These methods have achieved resultssuperior to classical heuristics in terms of makespanoptimization and energy efficiency [8], [10], [18].Nevertheless, the application of GNN-DRL in real-worldsystems still faces two core challenges. First, as the policynetwork continuously updates, the state embeddings in theexperience replay buffer become inconsistent with currentparameters, leading to Representation Shift, which weakensthe effectiveness of historical experience [14]. Second, HPCworkflows typically have long execution cycles, resulting inextremely sparse reward feedback [12], making it difficult foragents to obtain stable gradient signals during the earlytraining stages. These issues collectively constrain thestability and sample efficiency of DRL schedulers inengineering environments.C. Retrieval Augmentation and Explicit MemoryMechanismsTo mitigate the limitations of purely parameterizedpolicies in non-stationary environments, recent research hasbegun to focus on introducing explicit memory to enhance thestability of long-horizon decision-making. Retrieval-augmented mechanisms were initially used in NaturalLanguage Processing tasks [19]. Subsequently, works likeRA-DT [14] and ORA [20] demonstrated that utilizinghistorical trajectories for retrieval can effectively amelioratepolicy degradation in long-sequential tasks.However, traditional RAG approaches often rely on large-scale context processing, which is difficult to reconcile withthe latency-sensitivity requirements of online schedulingscenarios; meanwhile, generative scheduling methods [15]require processing additional contextual information duringinference, further increasing runtime overhead. Therefore,directly adapting retrieval mechanisms to HPC schedulingremains a challenge.In light of this, WASF-RAG adopts a lightweight design:state values retrieved from historical expert experience aremapped to a potential function and embedded into thereinforcement learning process via Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) [21]. As summarized in Table 1, this methodprovides dense rewards without altering the theoreticalpremise of the optimal policy, while avoiding the inferenceburden of large-scale context modeling. METHODOLOGYTo address the challenges in scheduling for multi-generational HPC—specifically complex task dependencies,sparse reward signals, and the non-stationarity of staterepresentations during online learning—this study proposesthe WASF-RAG (Weighted Adaptive Semantic FusionRetrieval-Augmented Generation) framework.As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework models thescheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Itutilizes a decoupled dual-stream Graph Neural Network(GNN) system to perceive the task graph (DAG) structure andcluster status, employs retrieved historical expert potentials toconstruct dense reward signals, and finally outputs theoptimized scheduling action distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) . Thissection elaborates on its mathematical principles across threecore dimensions: the Dual-Stream Graph Attention Encoder,Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), and the PPOOptimization Loop.Fig. 1. A. The Dual-Stream Graph Attention EncoderTo accurately capture the non-Euclidean topologicaldependencies between tasks, WASF-RAG discards thetraditional single-stream processing mode and innovativelydesigns a decoupled dual-stream architecture, as shown on theleft side of Figure 1. Both streams employ GATv2 (GraphAttention Network v2) [22] as the backbone network to rectifythe static attention defect found in standard GAT [23].Dynamic Feature Extraction based on GATv2: For anytask node 𝑖 and its neighbor 𝑗 in the DAG, GATv2 introducesa dynamic attention mechanism. Its attention coefficient 𝑒𝑖𝑗depends not only on the node’s static attributes but is alsodynamically computed based on the state of the current querynode:𝑒𝑖𝑗 = 𝐚𝑇LeakyReLU(𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛[𝑧𝑖 ∥ 𝑧𝑗])where 𝑧 is the linearly transformed feature vector, and ∥denotes the concatenation operation. This mechanism enablesthe encoder to precisely identify strong dependencies on thecritical path.Decoupled Stream Design and Anti-Drift Mechanism:To solve “Representation Drift” caused by parameter updatesin online reinforcement learning, the architecture is dividedinto two functionally orthogonal regions:• Policy Stream (Top Stream, 𝝓𝒑𝒐𝒍): As shown in Figure1, this module is marked as “Trainable / Online”. Itsencoder parameters 𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙 are updated in real-time withgradients, responsible for extracting transient featuressensitive to current decisions (such as instantaneouscongestion) and directly inputting them into theActor/Critic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) togenerate policies.• Retrieval Stream (Bottom Stream, 𝝓𝒓𝒆𝒕): This moduleis marked as “Frozen / Stop-Gradient”. Its parameters𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 are frozen immediately after initialization. Thisdesign constructs a time-invariant metric space,ensuring that the similarity calculation between thequery vector 𝑞𝑡 and the historical key vectors 𝑘𝑖 in theknowledge base is always based on the same basis,thereby guaranteeing retrieval consistency andpreventing index staleness.B. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)The “Interaction & Reward” module in Figure 1demonstrates how WASF-RAG utilizes the retrievalaugmentation mechanism to solve the sparse reward problem.Mixed-Strategy Potential Generation: The systemmaintains a Mixed-Strategy Knowledge Base (KB) storing“state-value” pairs generated by heuristic algorithms such asHEFT and Min-Min. At each time step 𝑡, the system retrievesthe Top-k neighbors via 𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 and uses a Softmax Attentionmechanism to calculate the potential value 𝛷(𝑠𝑡 ) of thecurrent state:𝛷(𝑠𝑡) = ∑ 𝛽𝑗𝑘𝑗=1𝑣𝑗, 𝛽𝑗 = exp(Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑗)/𝜏)∑ exp𝑘𝑚=1 (Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑚)/𝜏)where 𝜏 is the temperature coefficient. Crucially, theretrieved value 𝑣𝑗 ∈ [0,1] is defined as a composite qualityscore: 𝑣𝑗 = 𝑤1𝐼speed + 𝑤2𝐼eff + 𝑤3𝐼prog , integratingnormalized node speed 𝐼speed , execution efficiency 𝐼eff , andworkflow completion progress 𝐼prog.Here, 𝛷(𝑠𝑡) essentially quantifies the “potential value ofthe current state from the perspective of expert experience”.PBRS Mechanism and Optimality Guarantee: Toseamlessly integrate this offline prior knowledge into onlineRL, the architecture adopts a differential reward shapingformula:𝐹𝑡 = 𝛾𝛷(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝛷(𝑠𝑡)According to the theory by Ng et al., this form guaranteesthe policy invariance of the original MDP. This means theintroduced 𝐹𝑡 acts only as a “compass” to accelerateconvergence without restricting the agent from exploringglobal optimal solutions that surpass historical heuristic rules.C. Optimization Loop & Gradient DynamicsThe “Optimization Loop” on the right side of Figure 1illustrates the PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) [24]closed-loop feedback system based on the Actor-Criticarchitecture. This module transforms the features perceived bythe front-end into a specific probability distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡)and optimizes it via asymmetric gradient flow.Actor-Critic Network and Policy Generation: At the endof the Policy Stream (Top Stream), the extracted graph-levelfeatures are fed into the Actor MLP. This network outputs aprobability distribution 𝜋𝜃 (𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) over the action space,representing the probability of the agent selecting a specificnode for a specific task in state 𝑠𝑡:𝑎𝑡 ∼ 𝜋𝜃 (⋅ |𝑠𝑡)Simultaneously, the Critic MLP outputs the state valueestimate 𝑉(𝑠𝑡) to assist in calculating the advantage function.Advantage Estimation with Potential: In the optimizationprocess, the calculation of the PPO advantage function 𝐴𝑡 nolonger relies solely on the environment’s sparse raw feedback𝑟𝑡 , but incorporates the shaping term 𝐹𝑡 . Using GeneralizedAdvantage Estimation (GAE), the formula is as follows:𝛿𝑡 = 𝑟𝑡 + 𝐹𝑡 + 𝛾𝑉(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝑉(𝑠𝑡)This allows the policy update direction to be guided duallyby the environment’s real performance (𝑟𝑡) and the retrievedexpert potential ( 𝐹𝑡 ), effectively alleviating the cold-startproblem.Asymmetric Gradient Flow: The red dashed line(Gradient Flow) in Figure 1 clearly depicts thebackpropagation path of gradients, revealing the mathematicalroot of the architecture’s stability: Gradients start from thePPO Loss, updating the Actor and Critic network parameters.Gradients continue to backpropagate to the Policy Encoder

This indicates that themodel is not simply memorizing specific node labelsbut has learned a general Communication-Computation Trade-off pattern via the RAGmechanism.VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKThis paper proposes the WASF-RAG framework toaddress the challenges of complex task dependencies andsparse rewards in multi-generational HPC systems. To tacklethe non-stationarity of state representations during onlinetraining, we designed a Decoupled Dual-GNN architecture,establishing a stable metric space by freezing the retrievalencoder. Building on this, the framework integrates a mixed-strategy knowledge base with a Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) mechanism, transforming discrete historicalheuristic experiences into dense value guidance signals. Thisdesign not only ensures the convergence efficiency of deepreinforcement learning but also enables the agent toeffectively reuse high-value historical segments—includingthose from random exploration strategies—thereby breakingthrough the limitations of single heuristic rules.The high-fidelity simulation experiments based onWRENCH demonstrate that WASF-RAG achievescompetitive performance across multiple scientific workflows.Compared to the industry-standard HEFT algorithm, theframework achieves an average makespan reduction of 21.7%.Particularly in communication-constrained scenarios withsignificantly asymmetric I/O bandwidth (such as the Montageworkflow), WASF-RAG learns effective Data Localitystrategies, reducing makespan by 63.5% by proactivelyavoiding communication congestion. --- 第 1 页 ---
WASF-RAG: A Workflow-Aware SchedulingFramework with Retrieval-Augmented Generationfor Performance-Heterogeneous, Multi-GenerationalHPCAbstract—In multi-generational High-PerformanceComputing(HPC) systems, scientific workflow scheduling facesthe dual challenges of complex task dependencies and highlyheterogeneous resource performance. Existing heuristicalgorithms (such as HEFT and Min-Min) rely on staticassumptions, making them difficult to adapt to dynamicenvironments; meanwhile, although Deep ReinforcementLearning (DRL) holds potential for decision modeling, it haslong been constrained by issues such as slow trainingconvergence, sparse rewards, and non-stationarity in staterepresentation. To address these challenges, this paper proposesWASF-RAG, a retrieval-augmented scheduling frameworktailored for HPC. The framework reformulates scheduling as adecision sequence generation problem, utilizing a mixed-strategy knowledge base constructed offline to provide stablevalue priors for online learning. By decoupling therepresentation spaces of retrieval and policy, WASF-RAGensures metric consistency in experience reuse. Furthermore, itincorporates a Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)mechanism to transform retrieved historical expert trajectoriesinto dense feedback signals, thereby effectively overcoming thecold-start dilemma. High-fidelity simulation experimentsdemonstrate that in extreme scenarios with constrained I/Obandwidth, the framework autonomously learns Data Localitystrategies, reducing the makespan by up to 63.5% compared tothe HEFT algorithm. Ablation studies indicate that theproposed retrieval-augmented mechanism significantlyoutperforms pure DRL scheduling approaches, demonstratingclear performance advantages in extremely heterogeneousscenarios and effectively enhancing algorithmic robustness.Across extensive test sets, WASF-RAG achieves an averageperformance improvement of 21.7%, validating its effectivenessin complex dynamic environments.Keywords—Workflow Scheduling, Deep ReinforcementLearning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Graph NeuralNetworks, Potential-Based Reward ShapingI. INTRODUCTIONWith the rapid iteration of High-Performance Computing(HPC) hardware, modern data centers universally exhibit a"multi-generational" characteristic where new and legacynodes coexist, constituting a resource environment that ishighly heterogeneous and uneven in performance. Suchenvironments must support scientific workflows withcomplex dependencies—such as astrophysical simulations [1]and seismic imaging [2]—making scheduling onperformance-asymmetric resources with the objective ofminimizing makespan a typical NP-hard problem [3].The evolution of solutions to this problem has progressedfrom theoretical models to engineering heuristics. Earlyresearch mostly constructed theoretical models based onqueuing theory or linear programming. However, in realproduction environments facing issues such as I/O contention,network congestion, or multi-tenant interference, their staticassumptions regarding task execution times andcommunication overheads often fail to hold. Consequently,the industry has long relied on list-based heuristic algorithmssuch as HEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. Although these methodsare widely deployed due to their low computational overheadand ease of implementation, they are essentially rigidsimplifications of complex dynamic systems. Once real-worldscenarios deviate from preset models (e.g., encounteringsevere resource fragmentation or performance jitter), theperformance of such static methods declines sharply, leadingto significant efficiency losses [6].To break the constraints of static assumptions, theacademic community has begun exploring the use of DeepReinforcement Learning (DRL) and Graph Neural Networks(GNN) [7] to build data-driven schedulers. Methods such asGrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9] have demonstrated thepotential to surpass static rules in certain scenarios byperceiving topological structures and learning end-to-endpolicies [10]. However, such learning-based methods still facethe dilemma of sample-inefficient exploration in practicaldeployment. On one hand, the state representation of GNNsdrifts continuously as the policy updates (Non-stationarity)[11], making it difficult to effectively reuse historicalexperience. On the other hand, the inherent reward sparsity ofscheduling tasks [12], [13] leads to extremely slow modelconvergence. This often results in poor agent performanceduring the cold-start phase, making it difficult to meet thestrict stability and real-time requirements of productionenvironments.The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigmoffers a new opportunity to address the instability of theaforementioned sequential decision-making [14]. Themassive volume of high-quality scheduling logs accumulatedover long-term operations in HPC data centers actuallyconstitutes a rich, underexploited repository of decision-making data. Unlike high-latency generative schedulingmethods [15], we advocate using these logs as "externalmemory" to reuse historical expert experience via retrieval,while guaranteeing real-time inference. Based on this, thispaper proposes WASF-RAG—a retrieval-augmentedscheduling framework tailored for HPC.To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we designeda decoupled dual-GNN architecture: it utilizes a frozenretrieval encoder to construct a time-invariant metric space,ensuring the stable retrieval of high-value reference statesfrom the historical library. Simultaneously, it combines aPotential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) mechanism totransform retrieved expert trajectories into immediate dense

--- 第 2 页 ---
rewards, thereby effectively guiding agent exploration. Ourextensive experimental evaluation, conducted within SimGrid[16] / WRENCH [17] shows that WASF-RAG not onlypossesses performance comparable to the best heuristics understeady-state conditions but also exhibits significantadvantages in extreme heterogeneous scenarios withconstrained I/O bandwidth. By autonomously learning DataLocality strategies, it reduces the makespan by up to 63.5%compared to HEFT. This validates the effectiveness ofintroducing retrieval-augmented mechanisms into systemscheduling, providing a new pathway to solve the problems oflow sample efficiency and poor robustness in learning-basedschedulers.II. RELATED WORKA. From Static Rules to Dynamic Scheduling MechanismsIn multi-generational HPC systems, early researchprimarily relied on list-based heuristic algorithms such asHEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. These methods are widelyadopted in practice due to their controllable computationaloverhead and ease of implementation. However, assummarized in Table 1, such static methods heavily rely onestimates of task execution times and communicationoverheads, which are typically based on idealized assumptionsof the system state.B. Scheduling Methods based on Deep ReinforcementLearning and Graph Neural NetworksDeep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a pathway forend-to-end optimization in online scheduling. DeepRM [13]validated the feasibility of learning-based policies in resourceallocation scenarios, but its capability was constrained by alack of structural representation for task dependencies.Subsequently, works such as GrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9]utilized Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode thetopological structure of workflow Directed Acyclic Graph(DAG), enabling agents to make decisions guided bystructural information. These methods have achieved resultssuperior to classical heuristics in terms of makespanoptimization and energy efficiency [8], [10], [18].Nevertheless, the application of GNN-DRL in real-worldsystems still faces two core challenges. First, as the policynetwork continuously updates, the state embeddings in theexperience replay buffer become inconsistent with currentparameters, leading to Representation Shift, which weakensthe effectiveness of historical experience [14]. Second, HPCworkflows typically have long execution cycles, resulting inextremely sparse reward feedback [12], making it difficult foragents to obtain stable gradient signals during the earlytraining stages. These issues collectively constrain thestability and sample efficiency of DRL schedulers inengineering environments.C. Retrieval Augmentation and Explicit MemoryMechanismsTo mitigate the limitations of purely parameterizedpolicies in non-stationary environments, recent research hasbegun to focus on introducing explicit memory to enhance thestability of long-horizon decision-making. Retrieval-augmented mechanisms were initially used in NaturalLanguage Processing tasks [19]. Subsequently, works likeRA-DT [14] and ORA [20] demonstrated that utilizinghistorical trajectories for retrieval can effectively amelioratepolicy degradation in long-sequential tasks.However, traditional RAG approaches often rely on large-scale context processing, which is difficult to reconcile withthe latency-sensitivity requirements of online schedulingscenarios; meanwhile, generative scheduling methods [15]require processing additional contextual information duringinference, further increasing runtime overhead. Therefore,directly adapting retrieval mechanisms to HPC schedulingremains a challenge.In light of this, WASF-RAG adopts a lightweight design:state values retrieved from historical expert experience aremapped to a potential function and embedded into thereinforcement learning process via Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) [21]. As summarized in Table 1, this methodprovides dense rewards without altering the theoreticalpremise of the optimal policy, while avoiding the inferenceburden of large-scale context modeling. Thus, it offers anefficient scheduling pathway that simultaneously possessesstructural awareness and explicit memory mechanisms.TABLE I. COMPARISON OF REPRESENTATIVE WORKFLOWSCHEDULING APPROACHESMethod CoreParadigmTopologyAwarenessHistoricalKnowledgeAnti-Non-stationarityHEFT / Min-MinStaticHeuristicLimited(List-based) N/A N/ADeepRM Early DRL(CNN-based) Image-based ImplicitWeights N/AGrapheonRL /DRASGNN-basedDRLExplicitDAGImplicitWeights VulnerableWASF-RAG(Ours)Retrieval-AugmentedDRLExplicitDAGExplicitRetrievalFrozenEncoderIII. METHODOLOGYTo address the challenges in scheduling for multi-generational HPC—specifically complex task dependencies,sparse reward signals, and the non-stationarity of staterepresentations during online learning—this study proposesthe WASF-RAG (Weighted Adaptive Semantic FusionRetrieval-Augmented Generation) framework.As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework models thescheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Itutilizes a decoupled dual-stream Graph Neural Network(GNN) system to perceive the task graph (DAG) structure andcluster status, employs retrieved historical expert potentials toconstruct dense reward signals, and finally outputs theoptimized scheduling action distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) . Thissection elaborates on its mathematical principles across threecore dimensions: the Dual-Stream Graph Attention Encoder,Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), and the PPOOptimization Loop.Fig. 1. Overall architecture of the WASF-RAG system

--- 第 3 页 ---
A. The Dual-Stream Graph Attention EncoderTo accurately capture the non-Euclidean topologicaldependencies between tasks, WASF-RAG discards thetraditional single-stream processing mode and innovativelydesigns a decoupled dual-stream architecture, as shown on theleft side of Figure 1. Both streams employ GATv2 (GraphAttention Network v2) [22] as the backbone network to rectifythe static attention defect found in standard GAT [23].Dynamic Feature Extraction based on GATv2: For anytask node 𝑖 and its neighbor 𝑗 in the DAG, GATv2 introducesa dynamic attention mechanism. Its attention coefficient 𝑒𝑖𝑗depends not only on the node’s static attributes but is alsodynamically computed based on the state of the current querynode:𝑒𝑖𝑗 = 𝐚𝑇LeakyReLU(𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛[𝑧𝑖 ∥ 𝑧𝑗])where 𝑧 is the linearly transformed feature vector, and ∥denotes the concatenation operation. This mechanism enablesthe encoder to precisely identify strong dependencies on thecritical path.Decoupled Stream Design and Anti-Drift Mechanism:To solve “Representation Drift” caused by parameter updatesin online reinforcement learning, the architecture is dividedinto two functionally orthogonal regions:• Policy Stream (Top Stream, 𝝓𝒑𝒐𝒍): As shown in Figure1, this module is marked as “Trainable / Online”. Itsencoder parameters 𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙 are updated in real-time withgradients, responsible for extracting transient featuressensitive to current decisions (such as instantaneouscongestion) and directly inputting them into theActor/Critic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) togenerate policies.• Retrieval Stream (Bottom Stream, 𝝓𝒓𝒆𝒕): This moduleis marked as “Frozen / Stop-Gradient”. Its parameters𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 are frozen immediately after initialization. Thisdesign constructs a time-invariant metric space,ensuring that the similarity calculation between thequery vector 𝑞𝑡 and the historical key vectors 𝑘𝑖 in theknowledge base is always based on the same basis,thereby guaranteeing retrieval consistency andpreventing index staleness.B. WASF-RAG: A Workflow-Aware SchedulingFramework with Retrieval-Augmented Generationfor Performance-Heterogeneous, Multi-GenerationalHPCAbstract—In multi-generational High-PerformanceComputing(HPC) systems, scientific workflow scheduling facesthe dual challenges of complex task dependencies and highlyheterogeneous resource performance. Existing heuristicalgorithms (such as HEFT and Min-Min) rely on staticassumptions, making them difficult to adapt to dynamicenvironments; meanwhile, although Deep ReinforcementLearning (DRL) holds potential for decision modeling, it haslong been constrained by issues such as slow trainingconvergence, sparse rewards, and non-stationarity in staterepresentation. To address these challenges, this paper proposesWASF-RAG, a retrieval-augmented scheduling frameworktailored for HPC. The framework reformulates scheduling as adecision sequence generation problem, utilizing a mixed-strategy knowledge base constructed offline to provide stablevalue priors for online learning. By decoupling therepresentation spaces of retrieval and policy, WASF-RAGensures metric consistency in experience reuse. Furthermore, itincorporates a Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)mechanism to transform retrieved historical expert trajectoriesinto dense feedback signals, thereby effectively overcoming thecold-start dilemma. High-fidelity simulation experimentsdemonstrate that in extreme scenarios with constrained I/Obandwidth, the framework autonomously learns Data Localitystrategies, reducing the makespan by up to 63.5% compared tothe HEFT algorithm. Ablation studies indicate that theproposed retrieval-augmented mechanism significantlyoutperforms pure DRL scheduling approaches, demonstratingclear performance advantages in extremely heterogeneousscenarios and effectively enhancing algorithmic robustness.Across extensive test sets, WASF-RAG achieves an averageperformance improvement of 21.7%, validating its effectivenessin complex dynamic environments.Keywords—Workflow Scheduling, Deep ReinforcementLearning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Graph NeuralNetworks, Potential-Based Reward ShapingI. INTRODUCTIONWith the rapid iteration of High-Performance Computing(HPC) hardware, modern data centers universally exhibit a"multi-generational" characteristic where new and legacynodes coexist, constituting a resource environment that ishighly heterogeneous and uneven in performance. Suchenvironments must support scientific workflows withcomplex dependencies—such as astrophysical simulations [1]and seismic imaging [2]—making scheduling onperformance-asymmetric resources with the objective ofminimizing makespan a typical NP-hard problem [3].The evolution of solutions to this problem has progressedfrom theoretical models to engineering heuristics. Earlyresearch mostly constructed theoretical models based onqueuing theory or linear programming. However, in realproduction environments facing issues such as I/O contention,network congestion, or multi-tenant interference, their staticassumptions regarding task execution times andcommunication overheads often fail to hold. Consequently,the industry has long relied on list-based heuristic algorithmssuch as HEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. Although these methodsare widely deployed due to their low computational overheadand ease of implementation, they are essentially rigidsimplifications of complex dynamic systems. Once real-worldscenarios deviate from preset models (e.g., encounteringsevere resource fragmentation or performance jitter), theperformance of such static methods declines sharply, leadingto significant efficiency losses [6].To break the constraints of static assumptions, theacademic community has begun exploring the use of DeepReinforcement Learning (DRL) and Graph Neural Networks(GNN) [7] to build data-driven schedulers. Methods such asGrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9] have demonstrated thepotential to surpass static rules in certain scenarios byperceiving topological structures and learning end-to-endpolicies [10]. However, such learning-based methods still facethe dilemma of sample-inefficient exploration in practicaldeployment. On one hand, the state representation of GNNsdrifts continuously as the policy updates (Non-stationarity)[11], making it difficult to effectively reuse historicalexperience. On the other hand, the inherent reward sparsity ofscheduling tasks [12], [13] leads to extremely slow modelconvergence. This often results in poor agent performanceduring the cold-start phase, making it difficult to meet thestrict stability and real-time requirements of productionenvironments.The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigmoffers a new opportunity to address the instability of theaforementioned sequential decision-making [14]. Themassive volume of high-quality scheduling logs accumulatedover long-term operations in HPC data centers actuallyconstitutes a rich, underexploited repository of decision-making data. Unlike high-latency generative schedulingmethods [15], we advocate using these logs as "externalmemory" to reuse historical expert experience via retrieval,while guaranteeing real-time inference. Based on this, thispaper proposes WASF-RAG—a retrieval-augmentedscheduling framework tailored for HPC.To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we designeda decoupled dual-GNN architecture: it utilizes a frozenretrieval encoder to construct a time-invariant metric space,ensuring the stable retrieval of high-value reference statesfrom the historical library. Simultaneously, it combines aPotential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) mechanism totransform retrieved expert trajectories into immediate dense

--- 第 2 页 ---
rewards, thereby effectively guiding agent exploration. Ourextensive experimental evaluation, conducted within SimGrid[16] / WRENCH [17] shows that WASF-RAG not onlypossesses performance comparable to the best heuristics understeady-state conditions but also exhibits significantadvantages in extreme heterogeneous scenarios withconstrained I/O bandwidth. By autonomously learning DataLocality strategies, it reduces the makespan by up to 63.5%compared to HEFT. This validates the effectiveness ofintroducing retrieval-augmented mechanisms into systemscheduling, providing a new pathway to solve the problems oflow sample efficiency and poor robustness in learning-basedschedulers.II. RELATED WORKA. From Static Rules to Dynamic Scheduling MechanismsIn multi-generational HPC systems, early researchprimarily relied on list-based heuristic algorithms such asHEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. These methods are widelyadopted in practice due to their controllable computationaloverhead and ease of implementation. However, assummarized in Table 1, such static methods heavily rely onestimates of task execution times and communicationoverheads, which are typically based on idealized assumptionsof the system state.B. Scheduling Methods based on Deep ReinforcementLearning and Graph Neural NetworksDeep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a pathway forend-to-end optimization in online scheduling. DeepRM [13]validated the feasibility of learning-based policies in resourceallocation scenarios, but its capability was constrained by alack of structural representation for task dependencies.Subsequently, works such as GrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9]utilized Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode thetopological structure of workflow Directed Acyclic Graph(DAG), enabling agents to make decisions guided bystructural information. These methods have achieved resultssuperior to classical heuristics in terms of makespanoptimization and energy efficiency [8], [10], [18].Nevertheless, the application of GNN-DRL in real-worldsystems still faces two core challenges. First, as the policynetwork continuously updates, the state embeddings in theexperience replay buffer become inconsistent with currentparameters, leading to Representation Shift, which weakensthe effectiveness of historical experience [14]. Second, HPCworkflows typically have long execution cycles, resulting inextremely sparse reward feedback [12], making it difficult foragents to obtain stable gradient signals during the earlytraining stages. These issues collectively constrain thestability and sample efficiency of DRL schedulers inengineering environments.C. Retrieval Augmentation and Explicit MemoryMechanismsTo mitigate the limitations of purely parameterizedpolicies in non-stationary environments, recent research hasbegun to focus on introducing explicit memory to enhance thestability of long-horizon decision-making. Retrieval-augmented mechanisms were initially used in NaturalLanguage Processing tasks [19]. Subsequently, works likeRA-DT [14] and ORA [20] demonstrated that utilizinghistorical trajectories for retrieval can effectively amelioratepolicy degradation in long-sequential tasks.However, traditional RAG approaches often rely on large-scale context processing, which is difficult to reconcile withthe latency-sensitivity requirements of online schedulingscenarios; meanwhile, generative scheduling methods [15]require processing additional contextual information duringinference, further increasing runtime overhead. Therefore,directly adapting retrieval mechanisms to HPC schedulingremains a challenge.In light of this, WASF-RAG adopts a lightweight design:state values retrieved from historical expert experience aremapped to a potential function and embedded into thereinforcement learning process via Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) [21]. As summarized in Table 1, this methodprovides dense rewards without altering the theoreticalpremise of the optimal policy, while avoiding the inferenceburden of large-scale context modeling. Thus, it offers anefficient scheduling pathway that simultaneously possessesstructural awareness and explicit memory mechanisms.TABLE I. COMPARISON OF REPRESENTATIVE WORKFLOWSCHEDULING APPROACHESMethod CoreParadigmTopologyAwarenessHistoricalKnowledgeAnti-Non-stationarityHEFT / Min-MinStaticHeuristicLimited(List-based) N/A N/ADeepRM Early DRL(CNN-based) Image-based ImplicitWeights N/AGrapheonRL /DRASGNN-basedDRLExplicitDAGImplicitWeights VulnerableWASF-RAG(Ours)Retrieval-AugmentedDRLExplicitDAGExplicitRetrievalFrozenEncoderIII. METHODOLOGYTo address the challenges in scheduling for multi-generational HPC—specifically complex task dependencies,sparse reward signals, and the non-stationarity of staterepresentations during online learning—this study proposesthe WASF-RAG (Weighted Adaptive Semantic FusionRetrieval-Augmented Generation) framework.As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework models thescheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Itutilizes a decoupled dual-stream Graph Neural Network(GNN) system to perceive the task graph (DAG) structure andcluster status, employs retrieved historical expert potentials toconstruct dense reward signals, and finally outputs theoptimized scheduling action distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) . Thissection elaborates on its mathematical principles across threecore dimensions: the Dual-Stream Graph Attention Encoder,Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), and the PPOOptimization Loop.Fig. 1. Overall architecture of the WASF-RAG system

--- 第 3 页 ---
A. The Dual-Stream Graph Attention EncoderTo accurately capture the non-Euclidean topologicaldependencies between tasks, WASF-RAG discards thetraditional single-stream processing mode and innovativelydesigns a decoupled dual-stream architecture, as shown on theleft side of Figure 1. Both streams employ GATv2 (GraphAttention Network v2) [22] as the backbone network to rectifythe static attention defect found in standard GAT [23].Dynamic Feature Extraction based on GATv2: For anytask node 𝑖 and its neighbor 𝑗 in the DAG, GATv2 introducesa dynamic attention mechanism. Its attention coefficient 𝑒𝑖𝑗depends not only on the node’s static attributes but is alsodynamically computed based on the state of the current querynode:𝑒𝑖𝑗 = 𝐚𝑇LeakyReLU(𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛[𝑧𝑖 ∥ 𝑧𝑗])where 𝑧 is the linearly transformed feature vector, and ∥denotes the concatenation operation. This mechanism enablesthe encoder to precisely identify strong dependencies on thecritical path.Decoupled Stream Design and Anti-Drift Mechanism:To solve “Representation Drift” caused by parameter updatesin online reinforcement learning, the architecture is dividedinto two functionally orthogonal regions:• Policy Stream (Top Stream, 𝝓𝒑𝒐𝒍): As shown in Figure1, this module is marked as “Trainable / Online”. Itsencoder parameters 𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙 are updated in real-time withgradients, responsible for extracting transient featuressensitive to current decisions (such as instantaneouscongestion) and directly inputting them into theActor/Critic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) togenerate policies.• Retrieval Stream (Bottom Stream, 𝝓𝒓𝒆𝒕): This moduleis marked as “Frozen / Stop-Gradient”. Its parameters𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 are frozen immediately after initialization. Thisdesign constructs a time-invariant metric space,ensuring that the similarity calculation between thequery vector 𝑞𝑡 and the historical key vectors 𝑘𝑖 in theknowledge base is always based on the same basis,thereby guaranteeing retrieval consistency andpreventing index staleness.B. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)The “Interaction & Reward” module in Figure 1demonstrates how WASF-RAG utilizes the retrievalaugmentation mechanism to solve the sparse reward problem.Mixed-Strategy Potential Generation: The systemmaintains a Mixed-Strategy Knowledge Base (KB) storing“state-value” pairs generated by heuristic algorithms such asHEFT and Min-Min. At each time step 𝑡, the system retrievesthe Top-k neighbors via 𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 and uses a Softmax Attentionmechanism to calculate the potential value 𝛷(𝑠𝑡 ) of thecurrent state:𝛷(𝑠𝑡) = ∑ 𝛽𝑗𝑘𝑗=1𝑣𝑗, 𝛽𝑗 = exp(Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑗)/𝜏)∑ exp𝑘𝑚=1 (Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑚)/𝜏)where 𝜏 is the temperature coefficient. Crucially, theretrieved value 𝑣𝑗 ∈ [0,1] is defined as a composite qualityscore: 𝑣𝑗 = 𝑤1𝐼speed + 𝑤2𝐼eff + 𝑤3𝐼prog , integratingnormalized node speed 𝐼speed , execution efficiency 𝐼eff , andworkflow completion progress 𝐼prog.Here, 𝛷(𝑠𝑡) essentially quantifies the “potential value ofthe current state from the perspective of expert experience”.PBRS Mechanism and Optimality Guarantee: Toseamlessly integrate this offline prior knowledge into onlineRL, the architecture adopts a differential reward shapingformula:𝐹𝑡 = 𝛾𝛷(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝛷(𝑠𝑡)According to the theory by Ng et al., this form guaranteesthe policy invariance of the original MDP. This means theintroduced 𝐹𝑡 acts only as a “compass” to accelerateconvergence without restricting the agent from exploringglobal optimal solutions that surpass historical heuristic rules.C. Optimization Loop & Gradient DynamicsThe “Optimization Loop” on the right side of Figure 1illustrates the PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) [24]closed-loop feedback system based on the Actor-Criticarchitecture. This module transforms the features perceived bythe front-end into a specific probability distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡)and optimizes it via asymmetric gradient flow.Actor-Critic Network and Policy Generation: At the endof the Policy Stream (Top Stream), the extracted graph-levelfeatures are fed into the Actor MLP. This network outputs aprobability distribution 𝜋𝜃 (𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) over the action space,representing the probability of the agent selecting a specificnode for a specific task in state 𝑠𝑡:𝑎𝑡 ∼ 𝜋𝜃 (⋅ |𝑠𝑡)Simultaneously, the Critic MLP outputs the state valueestimate 𝑉(𝑠𝑡) to assist in calculating the advantage function.Advantage Estimation with Potential: In the optimizationprocess, the calculation of the PPO advantage function 𝐴𝑡 nolonger relies solely on the environment’s sparse raw feedback𝑟𝑡 , but incorporates the shaping term 𝐹𝑡 . Using GeneralizedAdvantage Estimation (GAE), the formula is as follows:𝛿𝑡 = 𝑟𝑡 + 𝐹𝑡 + 𝛾𝑉(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝑉(𝑠𝑡)This allows the policy update direction to be guided duallyby the environment’s real performance (𝑟𝑡) and the retrievedexpert potential ( 𝐹𝑡 ), effectively alleviating the cold-startproblem.Asymmetric Gradient Flow: The red dashed line(Gradient Flow) in Figure 1 clearly depicts thebackpropagation path of gradients, revealing the mathematicalroot of the architecture’s stability: Gradients start from thePPO Loss, updating the Actor and Critic network parameters.Gradients continue to backpropagate to the Policy Encoder

--- 第 4 页 ---
(𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙) of the Top Stream, enabling it to continuously adapt toenvironmental dynamics.Stop Gradient: When the gradient path reaches theBottom Stream, it is truncated by the “X” shown in the figure.This means the retrieval encoder 𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 is never updated by thePPO error signal. This asymmetric design mathematicallysevers the interference of policy updates on the retrievalmetric space, preventing index staleness caused by parameterupdates and ensuring the robustness of the entire learningprocess in dynamic environments.IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUPTo systematically evaluate the effectiveness of WASF-RAG on multi-generational HPC platforms, we constructed anexperimental protocol based on the high-fidelity simulation.All experiments were conducted in the WRENCHenvironment. WRENCH, based on the SimGrid kernel,accurately simulates computation latency, network contention,and I/O behavior, enabling the reproduction of complexscheduling scenarios without requiring physical clusterdeployment.A. Simulation EnvironmentThe experimental platform simulates a multi-generationalcluster with a three-tier architecture (configuration details inTable 2). The Core Tier consists of high-performance Ultranodes, representing the computing center of modern datacenters; while the Edge Tier contains Micro nodes withweaker computing capabilities.It is worth noting that to balance simulation efficiency withphysical realism, we adopted a proportional scaling strategy.Although the absolute bandwidth values in Table 2 are inMBps, this is intended to match the task computation amount(GFlops) which is also scaled down proportionally, therebystrictly maintaining the Communication-to-ComputationRatio (CCR) consistent with real scientific applications. Thissetting ensures that the simulation accurately reproduces therelative competition between computation and I/O in realscenarios, rather than merely pursuing absolute numericalalignment.TABLE II. Comparison BaselinesTo comprehensively analyze performance gains, weselected the following baseline methods:• HEFT & MIN-MIN: Represent classic static heuristicscheduling algorithms, focusing on earliest finish timeand system throughput, respectively.• WASF-DRL (Vanilla): A pure reinforcementlearning baseline based on GNN. This modelreproduces the core architecture of advanced DRLschedulers like GrapheonRL (i.e., GNN state encoder+ policy network) but removes the RAG and PBRSmodules proposed in this paper. Using this as acomparison aims to precisely quantify the performanceimprovement brought by the retrieval augmentationmechanism.• WASF-RAG (Full): The complete frameworkproposed in this paper, featuring retrievalaugmentation and mixed-strategy potential-basedreward shaping mechanisms.D. --- 第 1 页 ---
WASF-RAG: A Workflow-Aware SchedulingFramework with Retrieval-Augmented Generationfor Performance-Heterogeneous, Multi-GenerationalHPCAbstract—In multi-generational High-PerformanceComputing(HPC) systems, scientific workflow scheduling facesthe dual challenges of complex task dependencies and highlyheterogeneous resource performance. Existing heuristicalgorithms (such as HEFT and Min-Min) rely on staticassumptions, making them difficult to adapt to dynamicenvironments; meanwhile, although Deep ReinforcementLearning (DRL) holds potential for decision modeling, it haslong been constrained by issues such as slow trainingconvergence, sparse rewards, and non-stationarity in staterepresentation. To address these challenges, this paper proposesWASF-RAG, a retrieval-augmented scheduling frameworktailored for HPC. The framework reformulates scheduling as adecision sequence generation problem, utilizing a mixed-strategy knowledge base constructed offline to provide stablevalue priors for online learning. By decoupling therepresentation spaces of retrieval and policy, WASF-RAGensures metric consistency in experience reuse. Furthermore, itincorporates a Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)mechanism to transform retrieved historical expert trajectoriesinto dense feedback signals, thereby effectively overcoming thecold-start dilemma. High-fidelity simulation experimentsdemonstrate that in extreme scenarios with constrained I/Obandwidth, the framework autonomously learns Data Localitystrategies, reducing the makespan by up to 63.5% compared tothe HEFT algorithm. Ablation studies indicate that theproposed retrieval-augmented mechanism significantlyoutperforms pure DRL scheduling approaches, demonstratingclear performance advantages in extremely heterogeneousscenarios and effectively enhancing algorithmic robustness.Across extensive test sets, WASF-RAG achieves an averageperformance improvement of 21.7%, validating its effectivenessin complex dynamic environments.Keywords—Workflow Scheduling, Deep ReinforcementLearning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Graph NeuralNetworks, Potential-Based Reward ShapingI. INTRODUCTIONWith the rapid iteration of High-Performance Computing(HPC) hardware, modern data centers universally exhibit a"multi-generational" characteristic where new and legacynodes coexist, constituting a resource environment that ishighly heterogeneous and uneven in performance. Suchenvironments must support scientific workflows withcomplex dependencies—such as astrophysical simulations [1]and seismic imaging [2]—making scheduling onperformance-asymmetric resources with the objective ofminimizing makespan a typical NP-hard problem [3].The evolution of solutions to this problem has progressedfrom theoretical models to engineering heuristics. Earlyresearch mostly constructed theoretical models based onqueuing theory or linear programming. However, in realproduction environments facing issues such as I/O contention,network congestion, or multi-tenant interference, their staticassumptions regarding task execution times andcommunication overheads often fail to hold. Consequently,the industry has long relied on list-based heuristic algorithmssuch as HEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. Although these methodsare widely deployed due to their low computational overheadand ease of implementation, they are essentially rigidsimplifications of complex dynamic systems. Once real-worldscenarios deviate from preset models (e.g., encounteringsevere resource fragmentation or performance jitter), theperformance of such static methods declines sharply, leadingto significant efficiency losses [6].To break the constraints of static assumptions, theacademic community has begun exploring the use of DeepReinforcement Learning (DRL) and Graph Neural Networks(GNN) [7] to build data-driven schedulers. Methods such asGrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9] have demonstrated thepotential to surpass static rules in certain scenarios byperceiving topological structures and learning end-to-endpolicies [10]. However, such learning-based methods still facethe dilemma of sample-inefficient exploration in practicaldeployment. On one hand, the state representation of GNNsdrifts continuously as the policy updates (Non-stationarity)[11], making it difficult to effectively reuse historicalexperience. On the other hand, the inherent reward sparsity ofscheduling tasks [12], [13] leads to extremely slow modelconvergence. This often results in poor agent performanceduring the cold-start phase, making it difficult to meet thestrict stability and real-time requirements of productionenvironments.The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigmoffers a new opportunity to address the instability of theaforementioned sequential decision-making [14]. Themassive volume of high-quality scheduling logs accumulatedover long-term operations in HPC data centers actuallyconstitutes a rich, underexploited repository of decision-making data. Unlike high-latency generative schedulingmethods [15], we advocate using these logs as "externalmemory" to reuse historical expert experience via retrieval,while guaranteeing real-time inference. Based on this, thispaper proposes WASF-RAG—a retrieval-augmentedscheduling framework tailored for HPC.To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we designeda decoupled dual-GNN architecture: it utilizes a frozenretrieval encoder to construct a time-invariant metric space,ensuring the stable retrieval of high-value reference statesfrom the historical library. Simultaneously, it combines aPotential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) mechanism totransform retrieved expert trajectories into immediate dense

--- 第 2 页 ---
rewards, thereby effectively guiding agent exploration. Ourextensive experimental evaluation, conducted within SimGrid[16] / WRENCH [17] shows that WASF-RAG not onlypossesses performance comparable to the best heuristics understeady-state conditions but also exhibits significantadvantages in extreme heterogeneous scenarios withconstrained I/O bandwidth. By autonomously learning DataLocality strategies, it reduces the makespan by up to 63.5%compared to HEFT. This validates the effectiveness ofintroducing retrieval-augmented mechanisms into systemscheduling, providing a new pathway to solve the problems oflow sample efficiency and poor robustness in learning-basedschedulers.II. RELATED WORKA. From Static Rules to Dynamic Scheduling MechanismsIn multi-generational HPC systems, early researchprimarily relied on list-based heuristic algorithms such asHEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. These methods are widelyadopted in practice due to their controllable computationaloverhead and ease of implementation. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKThis paper proposes the WASF-RAG framework toaddress the challenges of complex task dependencies andsparse rewards in multi-generational HPC systems. To tacklethe non-stationarity of state representations during onlinetraining, we designed a Decoupled Dual-GNN architecture,establishing a stable metric space by freezing the retrievalencoder. Building on this, the framework integrates a mixed-strategy knowledge base with a Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) mechanism, transforming discrete historicalheuristic experiences into dense value guidance signals. Thisdesign not only ensures the convergence efficiency of deepreinforcement learning but also enables the agent toeffectively reuse high-value historical segments—includingthose from random exploration strategies—thereby breakingthrough the limitations of single heuristic rules.The high-fidelity simulation experiments based onWRENCH demonstrate that WASF-RAG achievescompetitive performance across multiple scientific workflows.Compared to the industry-standard HEFT algorithm, theframework achieves an average makespan reduction of 21.7%.Particularly in communication-constrained scenarios withsignificantly asymmetric I/O bandwidth (such as the Montageworkflow), WASF-RAG learns effective Data Localitystrategies, reducing makespan by 63.5% by proactivelyavoiding communication congestion. Ablation studies furtherconfirm that in environments with extreme resourceconstraints or significant heterogeneity (e.g., 1000x gaps), theretrieval augmentation mechanism is a key factor inpreventing the policy from falling into local optima andensuring scheduling robustness.Future work will focus on the following three aspects todeepen this research:• Real Machine Deployment and ConsistencyVerification: Current evaluations are based on ascaled-down simulation environment. --- 第 1 页 ---
WASF-RAG: A Workflow-Aware SchedulingFramework with Retrieval-Augmented Generationfor Performance-Heterogeneous, Multi-GenerationalHPCAbstract—In multi-generational High-PerformanceComputing(HPC) systems, scientific workflow scheduling facesthe dual challenges of complex task dependencies and highlyheterogeneous resource performance. Existing heuristicalgorithms (such as HEFT and Min-Min) rely on staticassumptions, making them difficult to adapt to dynamicenvironments; meanwhile, although Deep ReinforcementLearning (DRL) holds potential for decision modeling, it haslong been constrained by issues such as slow trainingconvergence, sparse rewards, and non-stationarity in staterepresentation. To address these challenges, this paper proposesWASF-RAG, a retrieval-augmented scheduling frameworktailored for HPC. The framework reformulates scheduling as adecision sequence generation problem, utilizing a mixed-strategy knowledge base constructed offline to provide stablevalue priors for online learning. By decoupling therepresentation spaces of retrieval and policy, WASF-RAGensures metric consistency in experience reuse. Furthermore, itincorporates a Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)mechanism to transform retrieved historical expert trajectoriesinto dense feedback signals, thereby effectively overcoming thecold-start dilemma. High-fidelity simulation experimentsdemonstrate that in extreme scenarios with constrained I/Obandwidth, the framework autonomously learns Data Localitystrategies, reducing the makespan by up to 63.5% compared tothe HEFT algorithm. Ablation studies indicate that theproposed retrieval-augmented mechanism significantlyoutperforms pure DRL scheduling approaches, demonstratingclear performance advantages in extremely heterogeneousscenarios and effectively enhancing algorithmic robustness.Across extensive test sets, WASF-RAG achieves an averageperformance improvement of 21.7%, validating its effectivenessin complex dynamic environments.Keywords—Workflow Scheduling, Deep ReinforcementLearning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Graph NeuralNetworks, Potential-Based Reward ShapingI. INTRODUCTIONWith the rapid iteration of High-Performance Computing(HPC) hardware, modern data centers universally exhibit a"multi-generational" characteristic where new and legacynodes coexist, constituting a resource environment that ishighly heterogeneous and uneven in performance. Suchenvironments must support scientific workflows withcomplex dependencies—such as astrophysical simulations [1]and seismic imaging [2]—making scheduling onperformance-asymmetric resources with the objective ofminimizing makespan a typical NP-hard problem [3].The evolution of solutions to this problem has progressedfrom theoretical models to engineering heuristics. Earlyresearch mostly constructed theoretical models based onqueuing theory or linear programming. However, in realproduction environments facing issues such as I/O contention,network congestion, or multi-tenant interference, their staticassumptions regarding task execution times andcommunication overheads often fail to hold. Consequently,the industry has long relied on list-based heuristic algorithmssuch as HEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. Although these methodsare widely deployed due to their low computational overheadand ease of implementation, they are essentially rigidsimplifications of complex dynamic systems. Once real-worldscenarios deviate from preset models (e.g., encounteringsevere resource fragmentation or performance jitter), theperformance of such static methods declines sharply, leadingto significant efficiency losses [6].To break the constraints of static assumptions, theacademic community has begun exploring the use of DeepReinforcement Learning (DRL) and Graph Neural Networks(GNN) [7] to build data-driven schedulers. Methods such asGrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9] have demonstrated thepotential to surpass static rules in certain scenarios byperceiving topological structures and learning end-to-endpolicies [10]. However, such learning-based methods still facethe dilemma of sample-inefficient exploration in practicaldeployment. On one hand, the state representation of GNNsdrifts continuously as the policy updates (Non-stationarity)[11], making it difficult to effectively reuse historicalexperience. On the other hand, the inherent reward sparsity ofscheduling tasks [12], [13] leads to extremely slow modelconvergence. This often results in poor agent performanceduring the cold-start phase, making it difficult to meet thestrict stability and real-time requirements of productionenvironments.The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigmoffers a new opportunity to address the instability of theaforementioned sequential decision-making [14]. Themassive volume of high-quality scheduling logs accumulatedover long-term operations in HPC data centers actuallyconstitutes a rich, underexploited repository of decision-making data. Unlike high-latency generative schedulingmethods [15], we advocate using these logs as "externalmemory" to reuse historical expert experience via retrieval,while guaranteeing real-time inference. Based on this, thispaper proposes WASF-RAG—a retrieval-augmentedscheduling framework tailored for HPC.To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we designeda decoupled dual-GNN architecture: it utilizes a frozenretrieval encoder to construct a time-invariant metric space,ensuring the stable retrieval of high-value reference statesfrom the historical library. Simultaneously, it combines aPotential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) mechanism totransform retrieved expert trajectories into immediate dense

--- 第 2 页 ---
rewards, thereby effectively guiding agent exploration. Ourextensive experimental evaluation, conducted within SimGrid[16] / WRENCH [17] shows that WASF-RAG not onlypossesses performance comparable to the best heuristics understeady-state conditions but also exhibits significantadvantages in extreme heterogeneous scenarios withconstrained I/O bandwidth. By autonomously learning DataLocality strategies, it reduces the makespan by up to 63.5%compared to HEFT. This validates the effectiveness ofintroducing retrieval-augmented mechanisms into systemscheduling, providing a new pathway to solve the problems oflow sample efficiency and poor robustness in learning-basedschedulers.II. RELATED WORKA. From Static Rules to Dynamic Scheduling MechanismsIn multi-generational HPC systems, early researchprimarily relied on list-based heuristic algorithms such asHEFT [4] and Min-Min [5]. These methods are widelyadopted in practice due to their controllable computationaloverhead and ease of implementation. However, assummarized in Table 1, such static methods heavily rely onestimates of task execution times and communicationoverheads, which are typically based on idealized assumptionsof the system state.B. Scheduling Methods based on Deep ReinforcementLearning and Graph Neural NetworksDeep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a pathway forend-to-end optimization in online scheduling. DeepRM [13]validated the feasibility of learning-based policies in resourceallocation scenarios, but its capability was constrained by alack of structural representation for task dependencies.Subsequently, works such as GrapheonRL [8] and DRAS [9]utilized Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode thetopological structure of workflow Directed Acyclic Graph(DAG), enabling agents to make decisions guided bystructural information. These methods have achieved resultssuperior to classical heuristics in terms of makespanoptimization and energy efficiency [8], [10], [18].Nevertheless, the application of GNN-DRL in real-worldsystems still faces two core challenges. First, as the policynetwork continuously updates, the state embeddings in theexperience replay buffer become inconsistent with currentparameters, leading to Representation Shift, which weakensthe effectiveness of historical experience [14]. Second, HPCworkflows typically have long execution cycles, resulting inextremely sparse reward feedback [12], making it difficult foragents to obtain stable gradient signals during the earlytraining stages. These issues collectively constrain thestability and sample efficiency of DRL schedulers inengineering environments.C. Retrieval Augmentation and Explicit MemoryMechanismsTo mitigate the limitations of purely parameterizedpolicies in non-stationary environments, recent research hasbegun to focus on introducing explicit memory to enhance thestability of long-horizon decision-making. Retrieval-augmented mechanisms were initially used in NaturalLanguage Processing tasks [19]. Subsequently, works likeRA-DT [14] and ORA [20] demonstrated that utilizinghistorical trajectories for retrieval can effectively amelioratepolicy degradation in long-sequential tasks.However, traditional RAG approaches often rely on large-scale context processing, which is difficult to reconcile withthe latency-sensitivity requirements of online schedulingscenarios; meanwhile, generative scheduling methods [15]require processing additional contextual information duringinference, further increasing runtime overhead. Therefore,directly adapting retrieval mechanisms to HPC schedulingremains a challenge.In light of this, WASF-RAG adopts a lightweight design:state values retrieved from historical expert experience aremapped to a potential function and embedded into thereinforcement learning process via Potential-Based RewardShaping (PBRS) [21]. As summarized in Table 1, this methodprovides dense rewards without altering the theoreticalpremise of the optimal policy, while avoiding the inferenceburden of large-scale context modeling. Thus, it offers anefficient scheduling pathway that simultaneously possessesstructural awareness and explicit memory mechanisms.TABLE I. COMPARISON OF REPRESENTATIVE WORKFLOWSCHEDULING APPROACHESMethod CoreParadigmTopologyAwarenessHistoricalKnowledgeAnti-Non-stationarityHEFT / Min-MinStaticHeuristicLimited(List-based) N/A N/ADeepRM Early DRL(CNN-based) Image-based ImplicitWeights N/AGrapheonRL /DRASGNN-basedDRLExplicitDAGImplicitWeights VulnerableWASF-RAG(Ours)Retrieval-AugmentedDRLExplicitDAGExplicitRetrievalFrozenEncoderIII. METHODOLOGYTo address the challenges in scheduling for multi-generational HPC—specifically complex task dependencies,sparse reward signals, and the non-stationarity of staterepresentations during online learning—this study proposesthe WASF-RAG (Weighted Adaptive Semantic FusionRetrieval-Augmented Generation) framework.As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework models thescheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Itutilizes a decoupled dual-stream Graph Neural Network(GNN) system to perceive the task graph (DAG) structure andcluster status, employs retrieved historical expert potentials toconstruct dense reward signals, and finally outputs theoptimized scheduling action distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) . Thissection elaborates on its mathematical principles across threecore dimensions: the Dual-Stream Graph Attention Encoder,Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), and the PPOOptimization Loop.Fig. 1. Overall architecture of the WASF-RAG system

--- 第 3 页 ---
A. The Dual-Stream Graph Attention EncoderTo accurately capture the non-Euclidean topologicaldependencies between tasks, WASF-RAG discards thetraditional single-stream processing mode and innovativelydesigns a decoupled dual-stream architecture, as shown on theleft side of Figure 1. Both streams employ GATv2 (GraphAttention Network v2) [22] as the backbone network to rectifythe static attention defect found in standard GAT [23].Dynamic Feature Extraction based on GATv2: For anytask node 𝑖 and its neighbor 𝑗 in the DAG, GATv2 introducesa dynamic attention mechanism. Its attention coefficient 𝑒𝑖𝑗depends not only on the node’s static attributes but is alsodynamically computed based on the state of the current querynode:𝑒𝑖𝑗 = 𝐚𝑇LeakyReLU(𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛[𝑧𝑖 ∥ 𝑧𝑗])where 𝑧 is the linearly transformed feature vector, and ∥denotes the concatenation operation. This mechanism enablesthe encoder to precisely identify strong dependencies on thecritical path.Decoupled Stream Design and Anti-Drift Mechanism:To solve “Representation Drift” caused by parameter updatesin online reinforcement learning, the architecture is dividedinto two functionally orthogonal regions:• Policy Stream (Top Stream, 𝝓𝒑𝒐𝒍): As shown in Figure1, this module is marked as “Trainable / Online”. Itsencoder parameters 𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙 are updated in real-time withgradients, responsible for extracting transient featuressensitive to current decisions (such as instantaneouscongestion) and directly inputting them into theActor/Critic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) togenerate policies.• Retrieval Stream (Bottom Stream, 𝝓𝒓𝒆𝒕): This moduleis marked as “Frozen / Stop-Gradient”. Its parameters𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 are frozen immediately after initialization. Thisdesign constructs a time-invariant metric space,ensuring that the similarity calculation between thequery vector 𝑞𝑡 and the historical key vectors 𝑘𝑖 in theknowledge base is always based on the same basis,thereby guaranteeing retrieval consistency andpreventing index staleness.B. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)The “Interaction & Reward” module in Figure 1demonstrates how WASF-RAG utilizes the retrievalaugmentation mechanism to solve the sparse reward problem.Mixed-Strategy Potential Generation: The systemmaintains a Mixed-Strategy Knowledge Base (KB) storing“state-value” pairs generated by heuristic algorithms such asHEFT and Min-Min. At each time step 𝑡, the system retrievesthe Top-k neighbors via 𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 and uses a Softmax Attentionmechanism to calculate the potential value 𝛷(𝑠𝑡 ) of thecurrent state:𝛷(𝑠𝑡) = ∑ 𝛽𝑗𝑘𝑗=1𝑣𝑗, 𝛽𝑗 = exp(Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑗)/𝜏)∑ exp𝑘𝑚=1 (Sim(𝑞𝑡, 𝑘𝑚)/𝜏)where 𝜏 is the temperature coefficient. Crucially, theretrieved value 𝑣𝑗 ∈ [0,1] is defined as a composite qualityscore: 𝑣𝑗 = 𝑤1𝐼speed + 𝑤2𝐼eff + 𝑤3𝐼prog , integratingnormalized node speed 𝐼speed , execution efficiency 𝐼eff , andworkflow completion progress 𝐼prog.Here, 𝛷(𝑠𝑡) essentially quantifies the “potential value ofthe current state from the perspective of expert experience”.PBRS Mechanism and Optimality Guarantee: Toseamlessly integrate this offline prior knowledge into onlineRL, the architecture adopts a differential reward shapingformula:𝐹𝑡 = 𝛾𝛷(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝛷(𝑠𝑡)According to the theory by Ng et al., this form guaranteesthe policy invariance of the original MDP. This means theintroduced 𝐹𝑡 acts only as a “compass” to accelerateconvergence without restricting the agent from exploringglobal optimal solutions that surpass historical heuristic rules.C. Optimization Loop & Gradient DynamicsThe “Optimization Loop” on the right side of Figure 1illustrates the PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) [24]closed-loop feedback system based on the Actor-Criticarchitecture. This module transforms the features perceived bythe front-end into a specific probability distribution 𝜋(𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡)and optimizes it via asymmetric gradient flow.Actor-Critic Network and Policy Generation: At the endof the Policy Stream (Top Stream), the extracted graph-levelfeatures are fed into the Actor MLP. This network outputs aprobability distribution 𝜋𝜃 (𝑎𝑡|𝑠𝑡) over the action space,representing the probability of the agent selecting a specificnode for a specific task in state 𝑠𝑡:𝑎𝑡 ∼ 𝜋𝜃 (⋅ |𝑠𝑡)Simultaneously, the Critic MLP outputs the state valueestimate 𝑉(𝑠𝑡) to assist in calculating the advantage function.Advantage Estimation with Potential: In the optimizationprocess, the calculation of the PPO advantage function 𝐴𝑡 nolonger relies solely on the environment’s sparse raw feedback𝑟𝑡 , but incorporates the shaping term 𝐹𝑡 . Using GeneralizedAdvantage Estimation (GAE), the formula is as follows:𝛿𝑡 = 𝑟𝑡 + 𝐹𝑡 + 𝛾𝑉(𝑠𝑡+1) − 𝑉(𝑠𝑡)This allows the policy update direction to be guided duallyby the environment’s real performance (𝑟𝑡) and the retrievedexpert potential ( 𝐹𝑡 ), effectively alleviating the cold-startproblem.Asymmetric Gradient Flow: The red dashed line(Gradient Flow) in Figure 1 clearly depicts thebackpropagation path of gradients, revealing the mathematicalroot of the architecture’s stability: Gradients start from thePPO Loss, updating the Actor and Critic network parameters.Gradients continue to backpropagate to the Policy Encoder

--- 第 4 页 ---
(𝜙𝑝𝑜𝑙) of the Top Stream, enabling it to continuously adapt toenvironmental dynamics.Stop Gradient: When the gradient path reaches theBottom Stream, it is truncated by the “X” shown in the figure.This means the retrieval encoder 𝜙𝑟𝑒𝑡 is never updated by thePPO error signal. This asymmetric design mathematicallysevers the interference of policy updates on the retrievalmetric space, preventing index staleness caused by parameterupdates and ensuring the robustness of the entire learningprocess in dynamic environments.IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUPTo systematically evaluate the effectiveness of WASF-RAG on multi-generational HPC platforms, we constructed anexperimental protocol based on the high-fidelity simulation.All experiments were conducted in the WRENCHenvironment. WRENCH, based on the SimGrid kernel,accurately simulates computation latency, network contention,and I/O behavior, enabling the reproduction of complexscheduling scenarios without requiring physical clusterdeployment.A. Simulation EnvironmentThe experimental platform simulates a multi-generationalcluster with a three-tier architecture (configuration details inTable 2).
